extra.message: Hardcoded/weak JWT signing secret — Attacker forges JWTs for any user_id, achieving full authentication bypass and impersonation of any account [verified: jwt.decode uses the hardcoded literal 'secret' at auth.py:23 with no environment-based override, so any attacker can sign a forged HS256 token with user_id set to any account and pass token_required.]

SQL Injection in registration — Arbitrary SQL execution: read/modify other users' data, forge balances, bypass constraints [verified: username/password_hash are f-string interpolated into a raw INSERT executed via db.session.execute with no parameterization or sanitization.]

SQL Injection in login — Authentication bypass, arbitrary data exfiltration from the database via UNION-based injection [verified: username is f-string interpolated into a raw SELECT executed via db.session.execute, enabling auth bypass/UNION extraction with no parameterization.]

IDOR: arbitrary password takeover via update-password — Full account takeover of any user by resetting their password [verified: update_password reads user_id from the JSON body and calls User.query.get(user_id) with no check against current_user.id or current password, allowing any authenticated user to reset any account's password.]

IDOR: arbitrary user password takeover via update-password — Any authenticated (or possibly unauthenticated, depending on route decorator) attacker can overwrite any other user's password by supplying their user_id, fully taking over their bank account [verified: Same as idx 3: /api/update-password trusts client-supplied user_id with no ownership check, enabling full account takeover of any user.]

Insecure YAML deserialization leading to RCE — Remote code execution on the server via crafted YAML payload [verified: profile_yaml from request body is loaded with yaml.Loader (unsafe full loader) instead of safe_load, permitting arbitrary object deserialization/RCE.]

SQL Injection and IDOR in get_transactions — Arbitrary SQL execution and cross-user transaction data disclosure [verified: user_id from request.args is f-string interpolated directly into raw SQL at line 49 with no parameterization, and no ownership check restricts it to current_user.id, enabling both SQLi and IDOR.]

SQL Injection in transaction search — Arbitrary SQL execution, extraction of other users' password hashes/PII via UNION-based injection [verified: search_term is interpolated unescaped into a LIKE clause via f-string at line 93, with no parameterization/escaping, allowing UNION-based injection.]

Client sends arbitrary user_id for password update, enabling IDOR on backend — An authenticated attacker can modify the outgoing request to submit a different user_id, causing the backend to change another user's password and take over their account [verified: Backend update_password (auth_routes.py:137-149) accepts user_id from request body and calls User.query.get(user_id) with no check against current_user.id, so any authenticated attacker can change another user's password.]

Hardcoded Flask/JWT SECRET_KEY — Attacker forges valid JWTs for any user_id, bypassing authentication entirely [verified: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'supersecret' at app.py:16 is a static checked-in value with no override from environment, usable for forging tokens/sessions.]

Insecure CORS: reflected Origin with credentials allowed — Cross-origin sites can perform authenticated requests on behalf of a logged-in victim and read the JSON responses (balance, transactions, PII) [verified: after_request (app.py:47-56) reflects any Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with no allowlist, permitting credentialed cross-origin reads.]

CORS reflects arbitrary Origin with credentials allowed — Any malicious website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the banking API on behalf of a logged-in victim and read the responses (account data, transfer funds via CSRF-like flow) [verified: Same after_request handler (app.py:47-56) reflects Origin header and sets credentials true, duplicate of finding 0.]

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY and debug mode enabled — If deployed with debug=True, exception pages expose the interactive Werkzeug debugger enabling remote code execution; hardcoded SECRET_KEY allows forging Flask session data [verified: SECRET_KEY hardcoded at app.py:16 and app.run(debug=True) at app.py:228 both present with no environment gating.]

Flask debug mode enabled in production-like deployment — Verbose stack traces leak source/config; if the debugger PIN is exposed or weak, an attacker gets an in-browser Python console for remote code execution [verified: app.py:228 explicitly runs with debug=True bound to 0.0.0.0, enabling the Werkzeug debugger on an externally reachable interface.]

Weak password hashing (unsalted MD5) — Trivial offline cracking of all user passwords once DB contents are exfiltrated [verified: Confirmed: password hashing uses unsalted MD5 in both models.py:24 and duplicated in auth_routes.py:21, no salting or slow KDF present anywhere on the auth path.]

IDOR via user_id parameter on transaction listing — Any authenticated user can enumerate and read any other user's transaction history (amounts, descriptions, transfer partners) by supplying a different user_id query parameter. [verified: Line 47 takes user_id from request.args defaulting to current_user.id but never validates it matches current_user.id, unlike get_transaction/search_transactions which scope to current_user.id, allowing IDOR read of any user's transactions.]

Transaction list request exposes user_id parameter enabling cross-account data access — An attacker can enumerate other users' transaction histories (amounts, counterparties, descriptions) by changing the user_id parameter, exposing financial PII across tenants [verified: backend/routes/transaction_routes.py:47 reads user_id from request.args and uses it in the query with no check against current_user.id, so an attacker can set user_id to another user's id and view their full transaction history (also SQL-injectable).]

Hardcoded weak default credentials and PII in seed data — Predictable seeded credentials allow trivial login to any demo account if this image/config is ever exposed beyond intended lab use, along with exposure of fabricated but realistic PII [verified: init_db() (app.py:76-224) seeds all demo users with identical weak password 'password123' and realistic PII (SSN, DOB, address) committed in source and loaded automatically at startup.]

Sensitive PII (SSN/DOB) exposed via profile endpoints — Disclosure of SSN and date of birth for any user whose token is obtained/forged [verified: get_profile/update_profile return full profile data (including PII fields) scoped only by current_user from the JWT; given the hardcoded weak JWT secret 'secret', tokens can be forged to access any user's PII.]

Unrestricted fund transfer / race condition on balance check — Concurrent parallel transfer requests can bypass the balance check (TOCTOU) allowing an attacker to overdraw and transfer more funds than they own [verified: transfer() has no locking/atomic update between the balance check (line 30) and the balance mutation (lines 33-34), and amount is unbounded, so concurrent requests can race past the check-then-act balance validation.]

Session token stored in localStorage instead of HttpOnly cookie — Any script-injection or malicious npm dependency can read localStorage and steal the JWT, allowing full account takeover (transfers, profile/password changes) without needing to steal cookies or bypass CSRF protections [verified: Token is stored exclusively via localStorage.setItem/getItem across App.js with no HttpOnly cookie alternative, so any XSS or compromised dependency can read it and hijack the session; genuinely missing control on a reachable path.]
